h1: Heel Pain Treatment in Kirkland, WA
summary: Heel pain is common, and it has several different causes. Finding the real source is the key to the right plan. Our Kirkland podiatrists look at your foot, your movement and your activity to guide care.

quickFacts.label: Common in
quickFacts.value: Runners, walkers, and people on their feet all day

quickFacts.label: Often felt
quickFacts.value: Under the heel or at the back of the heel

quickFacts.label: First step
quickFacts.value: Get the cause checked before you guess at a fix

overview: Heel pain is one of the most common reasons people visit a podiatrist. If you are searching for heel pain treatment in Kirkland, WA, the first thing to know is that the heel can hurt for many reasons. The pain may come from a band of tissue, a tendon, a nerve, a bone, or the fat pad under the heel.

The most common cause is plantar fasciitis, which often causes sharp pain with the first steps in the morning. Achilles tendon problems cause pain at the back of the heel. Heel spurs are often blamed, but many spurs do not cause pain. Stress injuries, nerve irritation and growth plate problems in kids can also play a part. Each of these needs a different plan, which is why a guess at home can lose time.

Where the pain sits, and when it shows up, gives strong clues. At Washington Foot & Ankle Sports Medicine, Dr. Lawrence Maurer and Dr. Kate Cryderman look at your feet, your gait and your training. We start with conservative care. Surgery is only discussed when it is the best option. This page links to our detailed guides. We see runners, hikers, parents and workers from Totem Lake, Bellevue, Redmond and across the Eastside.
symptoms: Sharp pain under the heel with the first steps after rest
Pain at the back of the heel, near the Achilles tendon
Heel pain that builds during or after a run
Tenderness when you press on the heel
Aching or bruised feeling after long days on your feet
Burning, tingling or numb feeling around the heel
Swelling or warmth at the back of the heel

causes.title: Plantar fasciitis
causes.text: Irritation of the thick band along the bottom of the foot is the most common cause. It often hurts under the inside of the heel, especially with the first steps of the day.

causes.title: Achilles tendon problems
causes.text: Overload of the large tendon at the back of the ankle can cause pain and stiffness just above the heel bone. It often follows a jump in running or hill work.

causes.title: Heel spurs
causes.text: A heel spur is a small bony growth. Many people have one and feel nothing. A spur may be present with heel pain, but it is often not the true source.

causes.title: Stress injury or fat pad irritation
causes.text: Repeated impact can bruise the heel pad or stress the heel bone. Pain often feels deep, and it may worsen on hard floors or with thin shoes.

causes.title: Nerve irritation or growth plate pain
causes.text: A pinched or irritated nerve near the heel can cause burning or tingling. In active kids, the growth plate at the heel can hurt, which is called Sever's disease.

diagnosis: Your visit starts with a talk about when the pain began, where it hurts and what you do each week. Then we check the heel, arch, ankle and calf for tenderness, tightness and strength. We often look at how you stand, walk or run, in person or on video, to spot biomechanical stress. X-rays or other imaging are used when the exam suggests a bone problem, a stress injury or something unusual. The goal is to name the true source of your pain so the plan fits you.

treatments.title: Relative rest and activity changes
treatments.text: We often adjust your training or work load for a short time so the area can calm down. You do not always need to stop moving, but you may need to change how much and how hard.

treatments.title: Stretching and strengthening
treatments.text: Targeted calf and foot exercises may reduce strain on the heel. We show you how to do each one and how to build up over time.

treatments.title: Supportive shoes and cushioning
treatments.text: The right shoe, heel cushion or arch support can ease load on a sore heel. We help you choose footwear that fits your foot and your sport.

treatments.title: Custom orthotics
treatments.text: When foot structure or movement adds stress to the heel, custom orthotics may help share that load more evenly. They are made from your exam and gait findings.

treatments.title: Physical therapy and other in-office care
treatments.text: Hands-on therapy and other conservative options may help calm pain and restore movement. Your plan depends on the cause we find. We may also work with a therapist when you need guided rehab.

treatments.title: Surgery when needed
treatments.text: Surgery is rarely the first step. It may be discussed if the problem does not improve with a full course of conservative care, or if the cause needs it.

whenToSeeUs: Heel pain that lasts more than a couple of weeks
Pain that is getting worse, or that wakes you at night
A heel that is swollen, red or warm
Trouble walking or putting weight on the foot after an injury
Numbness, tingling or burning around the heel
prevention: Increase running or walking distance slowly, not all at once
Wear shoes with good support and replace them when worn out
Stretch your calves often, especially after workouts
Mix hard surfaces with softer ones when you train
Do not ignore early heel soreness, since early care is usually simpler

faqs.q: Why does my heel hurt when I first get up in the morning?
faqs.a: Morning heel pain is most often a sign of plantar fasciitis. The tissue under your foot tightens while you rest, then stretches painfully with the first steps. It often eases as you move. Other causes are possible, so a foot exam can confirm the source and guide your plan.

faqs.q: What is the best heel pain treatment in Kirkland, WA?
faqs.a: The best treatment depends on the cause, so a proper exam comes first. For many people, conservative care works well. That may include stretching, better shoes, activity changes and custom orthotics. Our Kirkland podiatrists tailor the plan to your foot, your sport and your daily routine.

faqs.q: Is a heel spur the reason my heel hurts?
faqs.a: Not always. Many people have heel spurs and feel no pain at all. A spur may show up on an X-ray, but the pain often comes from nearby tissue like the plantar fascia. A full exam helps find what is truly causing your symptoms.

faqs.q: Should I keep running with heel pain?
faqs.a: It depends on the cause and how severe the pain is. Mild soreness may allow reduced running, but sharp or worsening pain is a sign to stop and get checked. Running through a stress injury or tendon problem can make it harder to recover.

faqs.q: When should I see a podiatrist about heel pain?
faqs.a: See a podiatrist if heel pain lasts more than a couple of weeks, keeps getting worse, or limits your daily life. Go sooner if you have swelling, numbness, or trouble walking after an injury. Early care often makes the plan simpler.

title: Plantar Fasciitis

h1: Plantar Fasciitis Treatment in Kirkland, WA
summary: Plantar fasciitis is irritation of the thick band under your foot. It often causes sharp heel pain with the first steps of the day. Most people do well with conservative care and a plan built for them.

quickFacts.label: Common in
quickFacts.value: Runners, walkers, and people who stand all day

quickFacts.label: Often felt
quickFacts.value: Under the heel, worst with first steps

quickFacts.label: First step
quickFacts.value: Calf stretching, supportive shoes, and a foot exam

overview: Plantar fasciitis is a top cause of heel pain, and many people look for plantar fasciitis treatment in Kirkland when it starts to limit their walks or runs. The plantar fascia is a strong band of tissue that runs from your heel bone to the base of your toes. It supports your arch each time you step. It is a very common problem, and it is often treatable.

When this band is overloaded, it can become irritated and sore. The classic sign is sharp pain with the first steps after sleeping or sitting. The pain often eases after a few minutes of walking, then may come back after a long day or a hard workout. Many people try to push through it at first. That can keep the tissue irritated and make the pain last longer than it needs to.

This problem is common in runners, but it also affects people who stand on hard floors at work. Tight calves, sudden jumps in activity, worn shoes and foot structure can all play a role. Dr. Lawrence Maurer and Dr. Kate Cryderman help you find the cause and treat it step by step. We see patients from Kirkland, Redmond, Bothell and across the Eastside.
symptoms: Sharp heel pain with the first steps in the morning
Pain after standing up from a long time of sitting
Soreness that eases with walking, then returns later
Pain along the inside of the heel or arch
Heel tenderness when you press on the spot
Pain that builds after running or long days on your feet

causes.title: Sudden jump in activity
causes.text: Adding miles, hills or speed work too fast can overload the fascia. The tissue needs time to adapt, and rapid change is a common trigger for runners and new walkers.

causes.title: Tight calf muscles
causes.text: Tight calves can limit ankle motion and raise the pull on the plantar fascia with each step. Many people with heel pain find their calves are tighter than they realize.

causes.title: Foot structure and movement
causes.text: Flat feet, high arches, or a foot that rolls in too much can add strain to the fascia. A gait and biomechanical exam helps show how your foot handles load.

causes.title: Footwear and surfaces
causes.text: Worn out shoes, flat soft shoes or long hours on hard floors may increase stress. Going barefoot on hard surfaces can also make symptoms worse for some people.

causes.title: Body weight and work demands
causes.text: Extra load on the feet, or jobs that require long standing, can add to irritation over time. This is one factor among many, and it is not the whole story.

diagnosis: We begin by asking when the pain started, what it feels like in the morning and how your training has changed. Then we press along the heel and arch to find the exact tender spot, and check calf tightness and ankle motion. We often watch you walk or run, in person or on video, to see how your foot moves. X-rays are not always needed, but we may use imaging if the pain is unusual, does not improve, or another heel problem is possible.

treatments.title: Stretching and strengthening
treatments.text: Calf stretches and plantar fascia stretches may ease pull on the heel. Foot and calf strengthening can build support over time. We show you what to do and how often.

treatments.title: Activity changes
treatments.text: We may suggest less running or standing for a short period, and a slow, planned return. The goal is to calm the tissue without losing all your fitness.

treatments.title: Supportive shoes and heel cushions
treatments.text: Shoes with good arch support and cushioning may reduce strain. We can help you choose footwear that suits your foot and your daily routine. A good fit matters as much as the brand.

treatments.title: Custom orthotics
treatments.text: If your foot structure adds stress to the fascia, custom orthotics may help support the arch and share load more evenly. They are based on your exam and gait findings.

treatments.title: Night splints and in-office therapies
treatments.text: Some people benefit from a night splint, taping, or other conservative therapies. We choose from these options based on your symptoms and how you respond.

treatments.title: Surgery as a last option
treatments.text: Surgery is uncommon. It may be discussed if pain stays strong after a full, well-done course of conservative care. We explain the pros and cons clearly first.

whenToSeeUs: First step heel pain that lasts more than two weeks
Pain that is getting worse instead of better
Heel pain that stops you from running or working
Sudden sharp pain with a pop or bruising
Numbness, tingling or swelling in the heel
prevention: Stretch your calves and arches often, especially after exercise
Build running mileage slowly, about a little at a time
Replace worn shoes and choose ones with good support
Avoid long stretches of barefoot walking on hard floors
Treat early arch or heel soreness before it grows

faqs.q: Why is plantar fasciitis worse in the morning?
faqs.a: The plantar fascia tightens while you rest overnight. When you take your first steps, it stretches suddenly and may hurt. Pain often eases as the tissue warms up. This first step pattern is a common sign, but a foot exam helps confirm the diagnosis.

faqs.q: Is plantar fasciitis curable?
faqs.a: Many people improve a lot with conservative care, but results vary and no one can promise a set outcome. Healing can take weeks to months. Staying with stretching, good shoes and a gradual return to activity gives you the best chance of lasting relief.

faqs.q: How is plantar fasciitis treated in Kirkland?
faqs.a: Treatment usually starts with conservative care. Our Kirkland podiatrists may recommend stretching, activity changes, supportive shoes and custom orthotics. We also check your gait to find what adds stress to your foot. Surgery is only considered if other options do not help.

faqs.q: Can I keep running with plantar fasciitis?
faqs.a: Sometimes, with changes. Mild pain may allow shorter, easier runs on softer surfaces. If pain is sharp, grows during a run, or lingers a day later, you should cut back and get checked. Pushing through can slow healing. We can help you plan a safe way to stay active.

faqs.q: How long does plantar fasciitis last?
faqs.a: It varies from person to person. Some people feel better in a few weeks, while others need several months. How long you have had it, your activity level and how well you follow the plan all matter. An early start on care often helps.

title: Heel Spurs
metaTitle: Heel Spur Treatment in Kirkland, WA | Run Doctor Podiatry

h1: Heel Spur Treatment in Kirkland, WA
summary: A heel spur is a small bony growth on the heel bone. Many people have one and feel nothing. If your heel hurts, the spur may not be the cause, so we look for what is really driving your pain.

quickFacts.label: Common in
quickFacts.value: Adults, often with long-standing heel strain

quickFacts.label: Often felt
quickFacts.value: Under the heel, or no symptoms at all

quickFacts.label: First step
quickFacts.value: Find the true cause with an exam and X-ray

overview: A heel spur is a small hook or shelf of extra bone that can form on the underside of the heel bone. It often shows up on an X-ray taken for another reason. If you are looking up heel spur treatment, the most important fact is this: a spur does not always cause pain. Many people are surprised by that.

Many people have spurs and never feel them. When heel pain is present, it is often caused by irritation of nearby soft tissue, such as the plantar fascia. The spur may simply be a sign of long-term strain in that area, not the thing that hurts. This is why removing a spur is rarely the first step. Most people do better when the real source of pain is found and treated with simple, steady care.

That is why a proper exam matters. At Washington Foot & Ankle Sports Medicine in Kirkland, we look at the whole foot, not just the X-ray. We check where it hurts, how you move and what you do each day. Treatment is conservative first, and it targets the true source of your pain. We see patients from Totem Lake, Bellevue and Woodinville.
symptoms: Sharp or aching pain under the heel
Pain that is worse with the first steps after rest
Tenderness when pressing on the bottom of the heel
Soreness after long walks, runs or standing
A feeling like a stone bruise under the heel
No symptoms at all, with the spur found on X-ray

causes.title: Long-term pull on the plantar fascia
causes.text: Repeated tension where the fascia attaches to the heel bone may lead the body to lay down extra bone over time. This is one common theory for how spurs form.

causes.title: Repeated stress from running and walking
causes.text: High mileage, hard surfaces and long hours on your feet can load the heel again and again. Spurs are seen more often in active people and those on their feet for work.

causes.title: Tight calves and Achilles tendon
causes.text: Tight muscles at the back of the leg can raise strain through the heel and arch. This extra pull may add to heel soreness and spur formation.

causes.title: Foot structure
causes.text: Flat feet, high arches or a gait that adds stress to the heel may play a role. A biomechanical exam can show how your foot handles load.

causes.title: Worn or unsupportive shoes
causes.text: Shoes with poor cushioning or support may let the heel take more impact. Replacing worn shoes is a simple step that often helps with heel strain.

diagnosis: We start by asking about your pain, your activity and your history. Then we press along the heel and arch to find the exact tender spot, and check how your foot and ankle move. A weight-bearing X-ray can show a spur, but we match the image to your exam, since a spur may be present without being the cause. We often study your gait too. This helps us decide whether the pain comes from the spur, the fascia or another heel problem.

treatments.title: Treat the true source of pain
treatments.text: Most heel spur pain is managed by treating the soft tissue around it, often the plantar fascia. We aim at the cause, not at the spur on the X-ray.

treatments.title: Stretching and activity changes
treatments.text: Calf and arch stretches, along with a short change in running or standing time, may help calm irritation. We guide a slow return to your usual routine.

treatments.title: Cushioning and supportive shoes
treatments.text: Heel cups, cushioned insoles and well-fitted shoes can reduce impact on a sore heel. We help you pick options that suit your foot and sport.

treatments.title: Custom orthotics
treatments.text: If your foot structure adds strain, custom orthotics may support the arch and ease load at the heel. They are made from your biomechanical exam.

treatments.title: In-office conservative therapies
treatments.text: Other conservative options may be added if needed, based on how your pain responds. We review each choice with you before starting. We explain the purpose of each step in plain words.

treatments.title: Surgery only when it is the best option
treatments.text: Surgery to remove a spur is uncommon. It may be considered if pain stays severe after a full course of conservative care and the spur is found to be the source.

whenToSeeUs: Heel pain that lasts more than two weeks
Pain that makes walking or running hard
Heel pain that keeps coming back
Swelling, redness or warmth around the heel
An X-ray that shows a spur and you are unsure what it means
prevention: Wear supportive shoes and replace them when they wear down
Stretch your calves and arches on a regular basis
Increase activity gradually, not in big jumps
Use cushioned insoles on hard work floors if you stand a lot
Get new heel pain checked early instead of waiting

faqs.q: Do heel spurs cause heel pain?
faqs.a: Often they do not. Many people have heel spurs with no pain at all. When the heel does hurt, the pain usually comes from nearby tissue, like the plantar fascia, not the spur itself. An exam helps tell the difference and guides the right plan.

faqs.q: Can a heel spur go away on its own?
faqs.a: A spur is bone, so it usually does not shrink or disappear by itself. The good news is that pain often improves without removing it. Treating the irritated tissue around the heel is typically the focus, and many people feel better with conservative care.

faqs.q: What is the best heel spur treatment?
faqs.a: The best care targets the real source of pain. For many people that means stretching, activity changes, supportive shoes and sometimes custom orthotics. Our Kirkland team checks your foot first, then builds a conservative plan. Surgery is only an option if other care fails.

faqs.q: Do I need surgery for a heel spur?
faqs.a: Most people do not. Conservative care is usually tried first, and many people improve with it. Surgery may be discussed only if pain stays strong after a full course of care and the spur is clearly the source. We explain all options first.

faqs.q: How do I know if my heel spur is the problem?
faqs.a: You cannot tell from an X-ray alone. A foot exam that finds the exact spot of pain, along with a review of your activity and gait, is needed. If your pain is around the spur and other causes are ruled out, it may be involved.

title: Achilles Tendonitis

h1: Achilles Tendonitis Treatment in Kirkland, WA
summary: The Achilles is the big tendon at the back of your ankle. It can become sore from overload, and in rare cases it can tear. Early care and a smart plan help keep you moving.

quickFacts.label: Often felt
quickFacts.value: Back of the heel or just above it

quickFacts.label: First step
quickFacts.value: Reduce load and get the tendon checked

overview: The Achilles tendon connects your calf muscles to your heel bone. It handles large forces every time you walk, run or jump. If you need Achilles tendonitis treatment in Kirkland, you may feel pain, stiffness or thickening at the back of your ankle. The tendon is strong, but it can be overloaded by too much work, too soon. Runners, hikers, skiers and weekend players often feel it first.

Doctors now often use the term Achilles tendinopathy. It describes a tendon that is struggling with overload, rather than only inflamed. Pain may sit in the middle of the tendon or low where it meets the heel. It is often stiff in the morning and warms up with movement. Pain with a gentle ache is common. Sharp pain with a sudden pop is different, so it helps to know which one you have.

A tendon that is only sore can often be managed with conservative care. But a rupture is different and needs urgent attention. Dr. Lawrence Maurer and Dr. Kate Cryderman check your tendon, your calf strength and your running form so we can match care to what you have. We see athletes from Kirkland, Bothell, Woodinville and across the Eastside who want to get back to training safely.
symptoms: Aching or burning pain at the back of the ankle
Morning stiffness in the tendon that eases with movement
Pain that grows during or after running or jumping
A tender, thickened spot along the tendon
Swelling at the back of the heel
Pain when pushing off or climbing stairs

causes.title: Sudden training changes
causes.text: Adding speed work, hills or mileage too quickly can overload the tendon. It adapts slowly, so rapid changes are a common trigger in runners and field sport athletes.

causes.title: Tight or weak calf muscles
causes.text: Calf muscles that are tight or lack strength may put extra stress on the tendon. Strong, flexible calves help the tendon share the work.

causes.title: Foot mechanics
causes.text: A foot that rolls in or out too much, or flat feet, may change the pull on the tendon. A gait and biomechanical exam can show these patterns.

causes.title: Footwear and surfaces
causes.text: Worn shoes, very flat shoes, or sudden switches to hard or hilly surfaces may add stress. Heel rubbing from shoe edges can also irritate the back of the heel.

causes.title: Age and past tendon problems
causes.text: Tendons change with age, and a past Achilles issue may make a new flare more likely. Staying active and strong helps support tendon health.

diagnosis: We ask when the pain began, what changed in your training and whether you felt any sudden pop. Then we check the tendon for tenderness, swelling and thickening, and test calf strength and ankle motion. We also look at your gait and foot mechanics. A simple calf squeeze test and strength checks help rule out a tear. Ultrasound or MRI may be used when the exam is unclear, symptoms are severe or a partial or full rupture is a concern.

treatments.title: Load management
treatments.text: We adjust running, jumping and hill work to a level the tendon can handle, rather than stopping everything. The plan builds back slowly as pain settles.

treatments.title: Strengthening exercises
treatments.text: Slow, progressive calf strengthening is a key part of tendon care. We guide the type, the load and the steps so the tendon can adapt safely.

treatments.title: Heel lifts and shoe changes
treatments.text: A small heel lift or a different shoe may reduce strain on the tendon for a time. We help you choose options that fit your foot and your sport.

treatments.title: Custom orthotics
treatments.text: If foot mechanics add pull on the tendon, custom orthotics may help improve alignment and share load. They are based on your biomechanical exam. They may be paired with calf strengthening for best effect.

treatments.title: Immobilization or other conservative care
treatments.text: For tougher cases, short use of a boot, along with other conservative therapies, may be used. We choose these options based on how severe your symptoms are.

treatments.title: Surgery when needed
treatments.text: Surgery may be an option for a ruptured tendon, or for a tendon problem that does not improve with full conservative care. We review all choices with you.

whenToSeeUs: A sudden pop or snap at the back of the ankle, which needs urgent care
You cannot push off, or cannot rise onto your toes
A gap or deep dent you can feel in the tendon
Pain, swelling or stiffness lasting more than a couple of weeks
Bruising at the back of the ankle after an injury
prevention: Build mileage, hills and speed work in small steps
Strengthen and stretch your calves each week
Wear shoes that fit well and replace them on time
Warm up before sprints, jumps and hard efforts
Back off early when the tendon feels sore or stiff

faqs.q: What is the difference between Achilles tendonitis and tendinopathy?
faqs.a: Tendinopathy is the newer term for a tendon that is sore from overload. Tendonitis suggests inflammation only, but many tendon problems involve changes in the tendon itself. In daily care, the terms are often used together. The plan focuses on load, strength and recovery.

faqs.q: How do I know if I tore my Achilles tendon?
faqs.a: A sudden pop or snap, sharp pain at the back of the ankle and trouble pushing off are red flags. You may also feel a gap in the tendon. If this happens, get urgent medical care. Do not wait to see if it settles.

faqs.q: Can I run with Achilles tendonitis?
faqs.a: Sometimes you can, with changes. Mild pain that settles quickly may allow lower mileage and flat ground. If pain is sharp, grows during the run or is worse the next morning, you should cut back and get checked. We can help you plan a safe way to stay active.

faqs.q: What is the best Achilles tendonitis treatment in Kirkland?
faqs.a: The best care depends on your tendon and your sport. Our Kirkland podiatrists often use load changes, calf strengthening, shoe changes and custom orthotics. We also check your gait to find causes. Surgery is only considered when other care fails or the tendon is torn.

faqs.q: How long does Achilles tendonitis take to heal?
faqs.a: Healing time varies. Mild cases may settle in a few weeks, while longer standing tendon problems can take months. Slow, steady strengthening matters most. Rushing back too soon is a common reason the pain returns, so follow your plan closely.

h1: Flat Feet Treatment for Adults in Kirkland, WA
summary: Many adults have flat feet and feel fine. For others, flat feet bring arch, heel, ankle or knee pain. We find out if your arch is a problem, and help you choose the right support.

quickFacts.label: Common in
quickFacts.value: Adults of all ages, and many have no pain

quickFacts.label: Often felt
quickFacts.value: Arch, inner ankle, heel, or knee

quickFacts.label: First step
quickFacts.value: Check if the arch is causing symptoms

overview: Flat feet, also called fallen arches, means the arch of the foot is low or touches the ground when you stand. Many adults have flat feet from childhood and never have trouble. If you are looking for flat feet treatment for adults, the key question is whether your arch is causing pain or problems. Not every flat foot needs treatment, and we will tell you honestly if yours does not.

Sometimes a flat foot develops later in life. This can happen from tendon wear, injury, arthritis, weight changes or long years on your feet. A sudden change in the arch, or pain on the inner ankle, is worth checking. It may involve the posterior tibial tendon, which helps hold the arch up. These changes often come on slowly, so they are easy to miss at first.

At Washington Foot & Ankle Sports Medicine, we look at how your foot works, not just how it looks. Dr. Lawrence Maurer and Dr. Kate Cryderman use biomechanical exams and gait analysis to see how your arch handles load. Care is conservative first, and surgery is only for select cases. Adults from Kirkland, Totem Lake, Redmond and Seattle visit us for arch and gait concerns.
symptoms: Aching or tired feeling in the arch
Pain along the inner ankle or inside of the foot
Heel pain or arch pain after standing or walking
The foot rolling inward when you walk
Shoes wearing down faster on the inside edge
Knee, hip or low back pain linked to how you walk
A change in arch shape over time, or swelling on the inside of the ankle

causes.title: Lifelong flexible flat foot
causes.text: Some people are born with a low arch that flattens when they stand. It is often painless, but it may become sore with heavy activity or long hours on the feet.

causes.title: Posterior tibial tendon problems
causes.text: This tendon supports the arch. If it becomes weak or worn, the arch may slowly fall, and pain may appear on the inner ankle. Early care is important.

causes.title: Injury or arthritis
causes.text: A past foot or ankle injury, or arthritis in the joints of the midfoot, may change the arch over time. These changes can bring stiffness along with pain.

causes.title: Weight, age and activity load
causes.text: Added body weight, aging tissues, and long hours of standing or walking can strain the arch. These factors do not cause flat feet alone, but they may add to symptoms.

causes.title: Tight calves and muscle weakness
causes.text: Tight calves or weak foot and hip muscles can change how the arch handles load. This can raise strain on the arch, heel and ankle.

diagnosis: We start with your story, including when you first noticed the flat foot and where it hurts. Then we examine your arch while you stand, sit and walk, and test the strength and flexibility of your foot and ankle. Gait analysis, in person or on video, shows how your foot rolls and how that may affect your knees and hips. Weight-bearing X-rays are used when we need to look at bones and joints, or when a tendon problem is suspected.

treatments.title: Supportive footwear
treatments.text: Shoes with a firm heel and good arch support often help. We guide you toward styles that fit your foot, your sport and your daily needs.

treatments.title: Custom orthotics
treatments.text: Custom orthotics may support the arch and improve how the foot shares load. They are made from your exam and gait findings, and they are a core part of care for many adults.

treatments.title: Strengthening and stretching
treatments.text: Exercises for the foot, calf and hip may help your arch work better. We show you a simple routine and adjust it as you progress.

treatments.title: Activity changes
treatments.text: We may adjust how much you run, stand or walk for a while if the arch is sore. A slow return to full activity helps prevent flare-ups.

treatments.title: Bracing or in-office care
treatments.text: If a tendon is involved, an ankle brace or other conservative therapy may be used to support the area while it recovers. We may also suggest guided rehab for the tendon.

treatments.title: Surgery for select cases
treatments.text: Surgery may be an option when pain or arch collapse does not respond to conservative care, or when a tendon or joint problem needs repair. We review all options with you.

whenToSeeUs: Pain along the inner ankle or arch that lasts more than a couple of weeks
An arch that seems to be falling or changing shape
Swelling on the inside of the ankle
Foot pain that limits walking, work or exercise
Knee, hip or back pain that may be tied to how you walk
prevention: Wear shoes with firm support and replace them when worn
Keep your calves flexible and your foot muscles strong
Build up activity slowly if you are new to running or walking
Avoid long hours in flat, unsupportive footwear
Get new inner ankle pain checked early

faqs.q: Are flat feet in adults a problem?
faqs.a: Not always. Many adults have flat feet and never feel pain. It becomes a concern if you have arch, heel, ankle or knee pain, or if your arch changes over time. A foot exam can show whether your flat feet need care.

faqs.q: Can flat feet cause heel and knee pain?
faqs.a: Yes, sometimes. When the arch lowers and the foot rolls inward, it may add strain to the heel, the inner ankle and even the knee. This is not true for everyone, so a gait exam helps link symptoms to your foot.

faqs.q: Do I need orthotics for flat feet?
faqs.a: Not everyone does. If your flat feet cause no pain, you may need nothing. If they cause symptoms, custom orthotics may help support the arch and share load. We decide based on your exam, your gait and your daily activity.

faqs.q: Why did my arch fall as an adult?
faqs.a: A newly flattening arch can be linked to the posterior tibial tendon, an injury, arthritis or long-term strain. It should be checked. Early care often gives you more options, so book a visit if you notice a change or inner ankle pain.

faqs.q: Where can I get flat feet treatment in Kirkland?
faqs.a: Washington Foot & Ankle Sports Medicine in Kirkland treats flat feet in adults. Our podiatrists use biomechanical exams, gait analysis and custom orthotics, and they start with conservative care. You can call 425-899-3234 to book a visit. Our office is in Kirkland near Totem Lake.
